pr_body:
This adds an "upstream" remote for the parent repository in addition to the "origin" remote. During an in-repo `repo fork` operation, an existing "origin" remote that previously pointed to the parent repo will now be renamed to "upstream" for consistency.

Fixes https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/582

Followup items:
- Decide whether and how to extend this behavior to the fork scenario in `pr create` as well.

issue_context.title: Update remote naming when using `gh repo fork` to use origin & upstream
issue_context.body:
When forking a repo with `gh repo fork`, the remote is named "fork". 

Instead I'd prefer this to use the upstream's namespace (username under which the fork lives), which, for a fork created by me, would be "waldyrious".

That would make the list of remotes more self-descriptive, and would allow cloning multiple forks of the same repo without naming conflicts or using e.g. counters like "fork-1", etc.

Note: the proposed solution is what `hub` does.
comments:
Thanks for adding your thoughts!

I agree that simply "fork" isn't the best name, partly because it's ambiguous (as you point out, there may be multiple remotes each pointing to _a_ fork). But I was also not perfectly happy with hub's default either, mainly for scripting: after issuing a `hub fork` operation, you would have to know your username to be able to generate a `git push <remote> <branch>` command. Later hub received the `--remote-name` option, which made it better for scripting so that you can pick a static name instead of having the remote be a moving target, but I still don't think the default is all that great.

Upon forking a repo, I'm leaning to naming your fork "origin" while renaming the other remote to "upstream". This goes along with "triangular workflow" that some in the git community are following and that GitHub generally encourages.

In the end, any default we choose will likely disappoint someone, and we're not yet ready to add a ton of configuration options for this either. So we're going to give this a lot of thought and update with new ideas/approaches.

We discussed this quite a bit this morning, and decided that we're going to follow the [documented GitHub model](https://help.github.com/en/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/configuring-a-remote-for-a-fork) here for remote naming of fork vs. parent.

When someone creates a fork, we'll use the following naming scheme:

Fork: `origin`
Parent: `upstream`

This sometimes means that the parent repo's remote will be renamed, many times from `origin`, to the new name, `upstream`. 

As @mislav mentioned, we know this isn't going to satisfy everyone, but we think it's a reasonable default and anything we do will likely not fit with everyone's preference.

😢

Thanks for considering this. I wish you had picked hub's approach, rather than one that will require renaming remotes and produce ambiguous remote names, but I trust that you weighted pros and cons of each approach.

#### Interoperability angle:
I have maybe hundreds of clone directories (on several machines) using hub's naming.  As `gh` doesn't cover (and doesn't plan to cover?) all of hub's functionality, I was thinking to use both, gradually leaning on `gh` more and more.  
But if they use different naming, I'll get a mixture of conventions, which is a recipe for me making mistakes.  
If `gh` starts renaming existing remotes, it's (1) surprising :-1: — in a sequence of `git push origin branch1; gh pr create; git push origin branch2` I don't expect `origin` to change meaning mid-way! (2) accelerates me getting a mixture of conventions.

- When renaming existing remotes, please make it print an attention-grabbing message.

- Consider a command for explictily normalizing remotes (and do nothing else).  Good for massive switch-over to new convention.

---

I really loved hub's naming, despite most my coworkers preferring `upstream` + `origin`.  Let me try to see why, and how new scheme compares.

#### History dependence
There are three and a half common scenarios:

1. Cloned upstream project as `origin`, never modified it.
2. Cloned upstream project as `origin`. Later decided to contribute, created a fork, adding a remote.
3. Directly cloned my fork as `origin`.  Later adding a remote for upstream.
4. Push / send PR to my own repo.  Only 1 remote, probably called `origin`.

It's is nasty that (1), (2) vs (3) result in `origin` meaning different things :-(

I felt that `hub` solved this problem, but did it really?  Not _exactly_.  
It's mainly that _any_ tool-supported convention encourages consistency!  I just learnt to ~avoid (2)~ EDIT: avoid (3) :smile:.  
However, `hub fork` did actively help, in several ways!  First, the habit of `hub fork` rather than doing it in the UI, gave me a "correctly named" remote.  Second, `hub fork` is idempotent, effectively alias to `hub remote add cben` if fork already exists.  This helped me avoid (3) by making it just-as-easy to always clone upstream, then add myself.  (Also removes any need to remember whether I'd already forked :sunglasses:)

#620 will be innovative and maybe even better :+1:

#### Symmetry with naming of other's forks

For repeated contributors, I like `hub add remote foo` adding their fork as `foo`.
I can have remotes `origin` (main repo), `cben` (me), `foo`, `bar`.  This is symmetric and nice :-)
Having remotes `upstream`, `fork` (me), `foo`, `bar` would be less symmetric :-\

(and as I said I enjoyed `hub remote add cben` for myself, although `hub fork` is shorter)

#### Scripting / shell safety

I work on projects where I have commit access to main repo, and sometimes collaborators' forks ("allow commits by maintainers" is nice!), but we want to always make PRs.
I taught myself to type `git push REMOTE`, not just `git push`.  Especially with `-f` :sweat_smile:.  But is remote name unambiguous?

- I have [a script](https://github.com/cben/myenv/blob/master/bin/git-ci) that boils down to `git citool && git push cben`.  

  Pushing to a remote named `cben` is never dangerous :construction_worker_man:.  If it exists, in scenarios (2), (3) it's my fork.  In scenario (4) I might want to be careful to open PRs and never push `master` directly, but my remote will be `origin` not `cben` (this relies on currently _not_ consistently naming it!) 

  Doing `git push fork` would be just as safe :+1:

  Doing `get push origin` is risky! :warning:  It might be my fork with new convention — but it risks being main repo or collaborators' fork, if I wasn't careful at `git clone` time...  
  I especially don't want to aquire the habit of `git push origin -f` during _normal contribution_ rebasing my PRs! :no_good_man: 

- Remote names are also important, even more, in branch refs.
  They **define what `origin/master` means** in commands!
  I type `git rebase -i origin/master` all the time.  Also `git diff origin/master` etc...

  Would `upstream/master` work just as well?  Mostly, yes.
  However, there is the case of (1) where I _didn't expect to contribute_, used off-the-shelf `git clone` and got it named `origin`...
  (Active renaming would mitigate this a bit :+1:)

----

#### Suggestion: `upstream` + `fork`.

`origin` is inherently ambiguous.  Globally it means "whatever I used in `git clone`".  Now it might mean "whether I'd used `hub` or `gh` in this directory".

Now you'll have a tool that knows how to query Github and [usually] figure out when it's dealing with main repo vs forks, which is an improvement :clap:  
=> Consider avoiding `origin` altogether and renaming to unambiguous `upstream` vs `fork`.  (Or `upstream` vs _username_.)

P.S. :heart: I'll use this opportunity to say Thank you — for `hub`, for `gh`, and for GitHub at large :)

> we're going to follow the [documented GitHub model](https://help.github.com/en/github/collaborating-with-issues-and-pull-requests/configuring-a-remote-for-a-fork) here for remote naming of fork vs. parent

Note that this document seems to be presuming that the workflow is something like

* navigate to someone else’s (e.g., an org’s) repo
* click the **Fork** button
* use the suggested commands under **Clone** to, e.g., `git clone https://github.com/myacct/repo`
* do work (preferably on a topic branch)
* file PRs, whatever
* optionally, at some point, add an `upstream` remote so you can merge in upstream `master`

whereas the command under discussion here invites a workflow more like

* find the name of someone else’s repo
* `gh repo clone someorg/repo`
* do work (preferably on a topic branch)
* `gh repo fork`
* `gh pr create`
* optionally, at some point, `git pull origin master:master` depending on the remote name (https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/847#issuecomment-626356064)
Is there some way to opt-out of this behaviour by default? (e.g. in config file?)

> Is there some way to opt-out of this behaviour by default? (e.g. in config file?)

https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/847#issuecomment-783708349 says:

```
$ gh alias set fork 'repo fork --remote --remote-name fork'
```

FYI this will update the config into `~/.config/gh/config.yml`

```
aliases:
    fork: repo fork --remote --remote-name fork
```

review_comments: ~this naming is confusing to me since it sounds like it's just talking about adding an entry with `git remote add`. If it's also going to clone maybe something like `createUpstreamRemote` would be better.~

Hmm, this function only literally adds a remote with `git remote add`, so I feel its name is in order. Cloning is done outside of the function, but `cloneURL` is passed so that the function knows how to `cd` into the proper git directory before executing `git remote add` (this is done via the `-C <dir>` git flag)
